The Armed Police Force recorded 25 incidents of religious or ethnic conflict between the fiscal years 2020-21 and 2023-24. But who is fueling the communal flare-ups in Madhesh?

An obvious suspect is the wave of communalism sweeping through the bordering towns in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh of India. The open border presents a significant challenge in containing the politicisation of religion, often sponsored by political parties, as is the case with India. The rise of the Bharatiya Janata Party has been concomitant with the shrinking of the secular public sphere in India, and this is no sheer coincidence. State-sponsored hatred of the Muslim minority has been a reality in the last 12 years, ever since the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh-backed BJP came into power. This has paid the party off very well: “Hindu khatre mein hain” (The Hindus are in danger) has been the most consistent political slogan of the BJP, which likes to use the suffix of ‘jihad’ against an entire community wherever it suits.

You don’t always need your apparatchiks to do the legwork: RSS’s brand of Hindutva has spilled over digitally as well, with Nepalis increasingly getting comfortable with the slogan “Jai Shree Ram”, replacing the local version, “Jai Siya Ram”. The politicisation of Hinduism on the streets of Madhesh last week has helped lay the groundwork for a return to Hinduism as a political principle. Once the road to the politicisation of religion has been paved and the secular fabric of the society torn, turning back becomes difficult, if not impossible. But turn we must. And how?

As the latest bout of communalism in Madhesh has shown, a state’s toleration of different religions does not automatically translate into religious tolerance in society. The Nepali state has certainly ensured the recognition and survival of Muslims as a political community; but it has, as of now, failed to secularise the society in a way that the Muslims feel acknowledged as the co-builders of the society itself. The state, therefore, must see to it that official secularism translates into a lived reality in Nepal. This begins with differentiating Hinduism as a cultural practice from its political offshoot, Hindutva, which is often intolerant and even violent—and replicating this for all religious communities.

Apart from the obvious operationalisation of political Hindutva in Madhesh, the current imbroglio is also the result of our internal failures at institutionalisation of secularism in the past two decades. If the tipping point came in the form of violence in Madhesh, the conditions had also been laid out in the vacuum of the public sphere left by political parties, successive governments and civil society. The Nepali state did the right thing by adopting secularism through the reinstated parliament in 2006, and then codifying it through the interim constitution of 2007 and the 2015 constitution. However, as Nepal’s political and civic spaces brimmed with debates over state restructuring, most vociferously over federalism, secularism remained just an et cetera.

Every political party shied away from talking about secularism, as if they had committed a crime by letting it seep into the interim constitution. Civil society members said in hushed voices that although secularism was a theoretical prerequisite for democracy, Nepali Hinduism wasn’t bad either. Antisecularists, thereby, kept abusing secularism as a foreign import imposed by NGOs to expand ‘foreign’ religions, including Christianity and Islam, and undermine Hinduism. In the absence of a sustained debate on the affirmative effects of secularism, common Nepalis have, therefore, felt that it was shoved down their throats, and hence a muted acceptance of the idea that Nepal can actually go back to Hinduism.

The communal flare-up this time has laid bare the fault lines of the official secularism we hastily adopted as the Nepali state’s political principle twenty years ago. It is now time to return to the beginning and establish that secularism isn’t a foreign idea sheepishly inserted into our constitution but a consciousness and a lived experience. Only when it becomes an integral part of our cultural praxis does secularism find its true meaning and acceptance.

articles.title: The persistent cycle of hope, expectation and dismay in modern Nepal
articles.summary:
Some notable features of modern Nepali history include the praxis of transition as well as people’s expectations, hopes and frustrations. This is indeed a feature of transition in the world. But in Nepal, as history shows, stories of dismay and unfulfilled expectations are mixed with dreams of change. We can see this pattern if we consider the major transitions that have occurred in the latter decades of the 20th century and the first two decades of the 21st century.

The transitions are notable for a few reasons. Political scientists, politicians (except a few) and social scientists have studied this subject. Many seminars and research projects are conducted, and academic theses are written on this phenomenon of transition in Nepal. It is beyond the scope of a short take and the subjective perception of a literary academic even to outline them. I want to share my personal impressions about the praxis of transition and the pattern of adjustment that recurs at intervals in modern Nepal. People of past generations saw and even experienced a number of praxes, and the younger generations have experienced a few of them. They have created some, we can say, as in the latest example of the Gen Z uprising.

The focus of every transition, interestingly and remarkably, is the people and the question of their rights. Every transition has projected people’s rights and bears testimony to their violations. An important instance has occurred in modern Nepali political and social history. This is surprisingly overlooked by both political parties and historians. I want to begin with a remarkable court hearing that is historical in a number of ways: BP Koirala’s court testimony in 1977. Following King Mahendra’s coup and the dissolution of Parliament in December 1960, Koirala and his colleagues, including Ganesh Man Singh, were put in Sundarijal prison. After his release in 1968, BP chose to go to India with his colleagues. He spent several years there before returning to Nepal in 1976 for some reportedly compelling reasons. Arrested again, BP was tried at a makeshift court.

It is important to revisit one important aspect of that testimony in today’s Nepal, when the question of people’s dignity in this country has become a motif of discussion. The testimony that BP gave in court is a very important political document that evokes the system of justice and democracy. There, BP questioned the legality of his arrest and the audacity of the king to strip the people of their democratic rights by dissolving the Parliament they had elected. A great theatrical or dramatic quality was in that court testimony, something that those working in theatre, including me, thought should be staged.

It was difficult to find this important document even among Nepali Congress people, which dismayed me then. A professor of political science, Krishna Khanal, gave me a photocopy of the document, based on which I wrote a play titled Sandajuko Mahabharat that was staged at Village Theatre under the direction of an NSD Delhi theatre graduate, Bimal Subedi. It was an entirely non-partisan theatrical exercise. Academic Sanjeev Uprety brilliantly played the role of BP alias Sandaju, and theatre artist Suryamala Sharma played the role of Sushila Koirala. Other young generation theatre artists successfully played the rest of the roles. We could not perform the play even for a month because of the Indian ‘embargo’ imposed under the order of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. That made it impossible for the audience to find public transport to come to see the play.

The highlight of the court hearing of BP is the written testimony he gave in court. Referring to the royal coup, BP said in front of the jury—the day the king staged the coup in December 1960, millions of Nepalis felt that they had lost their prestige; they felt demoralised. And that was a serious blow to the human rights and dignity of the people. I do not want to cite other arguments that BP Koirala presented at the court in his own defence as an individual defendant and a lawyer. That was the first time when a lawyer, a freedom fighter, had pleaded at the court on behalf of the entire people of Nepal. The question of prestige and the phenomenon of demoralisation deserve special mention today when Nepali people are fighting for the same.

That court hearing and the question of the dignity of people is the mantra of Nepali popular historical uprisings. But there is a pattern of people’s frustration that appears after every political transition in this country. The time of transition naturally brings euphoria, which does not last in that shape for very long. History shows that some patterns of people’s frustrations have some common roots. For a widely cited example, the system gets mired in practices commonly called corruption, indifference and injustice. After every shaking political change, people naturally wait for their government to come up with good plans and visions of amelioration.

But the experience shows that even realistic expectations of people are not addressed. Maitighar Mandala becomes agog with demonstrations of many groups who travel long distances to become visible and put their grievances to successive governments. That principally includes corruption, the settlement question, betrayal by moneylenders, educational conundrums and, most important of all, a sense of losing prestige or dignity. This may remind us of absurd plays staged by actors who are not heard and, painfully, they know that.

Many historical events have occurred in Nepal in the 21st century. One important element of these praxes is the transition to democratic rule. The present multiparty republican constitution, which may require necessary reviews and amendments in the course of time, represents a solid example of the spirit of transition. The diverse approaches to political change meet at a common platform. The Parliament is such a forum where the erstwhile Maoist guerrillas, the Nepali Congress, the various factions of the communists of Nepal, the advocates of the abolished monarchical system, and, more recently, the Rastriya Swatantra Party, which won a majority in the general election and includes Gen Zers, all meet and discuss, though this does not appear to be happening as expected. Judging by the praxis of change, we can say that democratic history has not ended in Nepal.

articles.title: Lift the migration ban on domestic work
articles.summary:
Nepal remembers women migrant domestic workers exist when their remittances arrive home. However, it forgets them when they seek support from the state. Somewhere in West Asia, a poor Dalit Nepali domestic worker is fulfilling the care needs of a household. Driven not only by gender- and caste-based oppression at home but also by the lack of economic opportunities in the country, she sustains households in the Gulf, contributes to Nepal through remittances, helps her family escape intergenerational caste oppression, and invests in the next generation of Nepali citizens.

While she is legal in the country where she works, she is invisible in the country to which she ‘belongs’, having migrated without the government-issued ‘labour permit’. By refusing to recognise her labour migration, the state has chosen to evade its responsibility towards her, thereby rendering her disposable.

Nepal’s migration bans on domestic work push women into precarious and undocumented journeys, making them invisible to the state that bears a constitutional duty to protect its most marginalised citizens. If she suffers exploitation, abuse, disappearance or even death, the state has no official record that she ever migrated. It excludes her from consular protection, accountability and pathways to redress against exploitation. In effect, she is punished for navigating the very deficit in state care, opportunity, welfare and protection from gender-based violence that thousands of women confront every day.

Yet for 25 years, successive governments have waged a war against women’s migration into domestic work whilst failing to confront exploitation within that sector. They have mistaken Nepali women’s mobility for the problem, turning some of the most marginalised citizens into the targets of state restriction and confinement. Their solution has been to prevent Nepali women from migrating, resulting in successive bans on domestic work migration.

However, research from Nepal and countries such as Sri Lanka, Indonesia, the Philippines and Bangladesh challenges this assumption. It shows that migration into domestic work is neither inherently nor exceptionally exploitative. Instead, exploitation is embedded across migrant labour regimes, with male migrant workers from these countries experiencing exploitation that is often comparable to, or even more severe than, that experienced by women domestic workers.

Research suggests no ban can stop determined Nepali women from migrating. The ban prevents the state from knowing about their migration, abandons thousands of women who are working as domestic workers, and absolves the state from being obliged to respond when things go wrong.

More recently, Nepal imposed a blanket migration ban in 2017. This total ban on migration for domestic work followed a field visit by and recommendation from a parliamentary committee. These parliamentary committees carry institutional weight, but their decisions are not fixed; they can revise recommendations when new evidence or circumstances demand it.

For example, the committee in 2020 recommended seven preconditions for lifting the migration ban, the most important being the presence of a dedicated Bilateral Labour Agreement (BLA) on domestic work with a host country. In practice, this has functioned as an indefinite postponement, since most of the preconditions lie largely beyond what Nepal can secure on its own.

These preconditions have become an instrument of state abandonment, enabling the government to evade its constitutional obligations whilst thousands of already marginalised citizens continue to bear the consequences.

Even where BLAs exist, they have not delivered what is claimed. Nepal already has BLAs with several destination countries where migrant workers continue to face degrees and forms of labour exploitation and abuse. Hence, a signed agreement alone cannot guarantee safe working conditions.

Nine years on, we now have a substantial body of evidence about what the ban actually produced: growth in irregular migration, greater exposure to abuse and exploitation, invisible and premature deaths, and the denial of safe and regulated employment to thousands of women. This evidence should prompt a parliamentary committee to revisit earlier recommendations.

Consider the numbers: In the first 10 months of the last fiscal year, 1,273 Nepali migrant workers returned home in coffins. Of these, 1,229 were men and only 44 were women. These figures cover only migrants who travelled through formal channels; the deaths of women who migrated informally are not counted at all. Nepali men’s deaths in sectors such as Qatari construction have occurred at a comparable or greater scale, yet this has never led to a ban on men’s mobility. Only women’s migration into domestic work has been treated this way, an asymmetry that traces back to the 1985 Foreign Employment Act, which required women to obtain a male guardian’s permission to migrate.

Yet, the ban fails to keep Nepali women at home. Estimates suggest that between 60,000 and 100,000 Nepali women currently work as domestic workers in the Gulf, most through informal channels, and this may understate the actual figures, given how much of migration in domestic work is invisible.

An ILO report suggests that when the ban was briefly lifted in 2010, the proportion of women migrating through legal channels tripled. This highlights that women are migrating at similarly high rates, only now without a labour contract, registration with Nepali missions abroad, consular assistance and any route to compensation if they are injured or killed.

Civil society groups, returnee workers and concerned Nepali citizens should consider a formal route open to them now: a petition to the Women and Social Affairs Committee and the Law, Justice and Human Rights Committee, requesting a review of the ban on the grounds of women’s rights, labour migration, human rights and access to safe employment. This migration ban must be revisited in light of nearly a decade of evidence showing that it has failed to serve the purpose for which it was designed.

None of this suggests domestic work abroad is free of risk, or that bilateral agreements and other preconditions have no value. BLAs, embassy capacity, recruitment reform and compensation systems should be built after the ban is lifted. For nine years, these preconditions have allowed the state to wash its hands of thousands of marginalised Nepali women who care for families abroad and sustain households at home through remittances, yet officially do not exist as migrant workers in the eyes of the state to which they belong.

The committees that recommended this ban in 2017 acted within their authority and, one assumes, in good faith. Parliament cannot continue claiming to protect women whilst defending a policy that leaves thousands beyond the protection of the Nepali state. Hence, the choice before Parliament is whether it will accept responsibility for a policy that has exposed thousands of Nepali women to abuse, exploitation and death, while making their suffering invisible to the very state responsible for protecting them.

articles.title: The intersection of art and human psyche at Annapurna Gallery
articles.summary:
‘Chromatic Psyche: A Collective Art Show’, curated by Roshan Bhandari and exhibited at Annapurna Gallery, brings together the distinct visual practices of nine contemporary artists. Featuring 36 original works spanning painting, mixed media, and ceramic sculpture, the exhibition explores a rich spectrum of artistic expression through diverse materials, techniques, and perspectives. The show runs until August 23.

At the heart of the exhibit is an exploration of the human psyche through colour, memory, emotion, and lived experience. While each artist presents a distinct perspective, the exhibition forms a compelling dialogue where personal narratives intersect with themes of identity, nature, cultural heritage, and contemporary society.

The exhibited works employ a wide range of materials and techniques, demonstrating how artistic mediums can become powerful mediums for thought and emotion. Nature appears throughout the exhibition as memories and metaphors, while symbolic imagery explores themes of womanhood, vulnerability, compassion, urban transformation, cultural

preservation, and the complexities of the inner self.

Rather than presenting a single narrative, ‘Chromatic Psyche’ celebrates the diversity of contemporary artistic expression. Each artwork engages with a unique psychological landscape, inviting viewers to reflect on their own emotions, memories, and perceptions.

—————————————————————————————-

Chromatic Psyche: A Collective Art Show

Date: Until August 23

Where: Annapurna Gallery, Radhe Radhe, Bhaktapur

Time: 10:00 AM – 7:00 PM

Entrance: Free

articles.title: Deepmala Dhakal crowned as the Miss Nepal 2026
articles.summary:
Deepmala Dhakal won the Miss Nepal World 2026 title at the grand finale held at The Plaza in Pulchowk, Lalitpur, on Saturday, where the event showcased this year’s theme, ‘Top of the World’, a tribute to Nepal’s mountainous heritage and the aspirations of contestants seeking to reach the global stage.

The night's emotional peak arrived with the crowning of Deepmala as Miss Nepal World 2026, Arya Nishaant as Miss Nepal International 2026 and Kashis Subba as Miss Nepal Cosmo 2026. Each crowning was met with confetti, cheers and thunderous applause.

Answering a query Deepmala said she was inspired by her mother, who competed in the first Miss Nepal competition held in 1994. The 24-year-old works as an investment strategist at global investment management firm BlackRock. She is also a taekwondo black belt holder, a marathon runner, and has completed her bachelor’s degree in economics.

The event began with a tribute to mountaineers from around the globe. A mix of participants, past titleholders, family members and pageant devotees filled every seat with anticipation.

After the introduction of The Hidden Treasure's board of directors, an enchanting dance performance titled Mountain Silhouette followed, with the 24 finalists taking the stage in intricately choreographed routines.

With hosts Sanjay Silwal Gupta and Roneeshma Shrestha addressing the crowd, ‘The Hidden Treasure Kajaria Miss Nepal 2026’ commended the 24 finalists announcing their name, age and homeland with their riveting voices that held immense pride. This was one of the night's most breathtaking moments. All 24 finalists walked on the stage in Manish Rai’s designs. Each entrance’s celebration was amplified by a burst of applause.

This year's class was a striking one: doctors, lawyers, civil engineers, and past titleholders shared the stage.

With much anticipation, the subtitle awards were announced. Kashis Subba won the ‘Kajaria Miss Top Model’, Prema Lamgade bagged ‘Xiaomi Miss Multimedia’, Shraddha Adhikari won the ‘Xtreme Energy Miss Active’, Deepmala Dhakal was entitled ‘BYD Miss Green Visionary’ and also the ‘Nepal Medicity Miss Health and Harmony’.

Thereafter, the emcees introduced this year’s judges — Yolina Lindquist, Rupesh Pradhan, Srichchha Pradhan, Birendra Raj Pandey, Purnima Shrestha, Sarik Bogati, Recha Shrestha, Jitendra Bahadur Chand and Rajani Thapa.

The energy sharpened considerably once the Top 12 were announced. Prema Lamgada, Arbisha Thapa, Shraddha Adhikari, Deepmala Dhakal, Kashis Subba, Arya Nishaant, Swikriti Gyawali, Sezja Shrestha, Shreeyashi Shrestha, Anshu Kunwar, Bibusha Baasnet and Dr Shitanshu Dhakal. The showcase began with individual walks, each finalist given their moment under the spotlight, drawing every eye forward.

A dedicated Miss Cosmo segment added a jolt of glamour mid-showcase, and the arrival of distinguished guests was marked with its own ripple of applause through the crowd.

Within this celebration, a question emerged, “Who will earn the place in the top 6?”

Once again, the 24 contestants graced the stage with gowns designed by Rai and inspired by Kajaria tiles, capturing the audience's attention with sparkling glitters and coutures tailored to complement every silhouette.

Back again to the subtitle awards, the ‘Dabur Vatika Miss Beautiful Hair’ was granted to Shreeyashi Shrestha. Similarly, Shitanshu Dhakal was entitled ‘The Kathmandu Post Miss Intellectual. ‘Brij Cement Miss Confident’ was awarded to Deepmala Dhakal, Chadani Shrestha won ‘Farmasi Face of the year’ and the title ‘Miss DHI’ went to Sangita Paudel.

Similarly, Shitanshu Dhakal was entitled ‘National Live Miss Empowered Choices’ and Sezja Shrestha was known to be the ‘ENBIO Miss Pristine’, ‘Shree Natraj Miss Sparkling Diva’ was given to Prema Lamgada and finally, as a result of the rigorous voting process from the public, Arbisha Thapa won the ‘Real Miss Popular Choice’ award.

Moving to the moment of expectancy, the top 6 participants were announced with the crowd’s loudest cheers so far. Finalists included Shitanshu Dhakal, Kashis Subba, Deepmala Dhakal, Swikriti Gyawali, Arya Nishaant and Bibhusha Basnet.

The mood intensified as they faced the final question and answer round. This round, as per the hosts, defines the legacy of Miss Nepal.

Pin drop silence engulfed the hall as the finalists picked their questions and were given seconds to answer. This segment carried extra weight given organisers' decision to retain the traditional top-13 question-and-answer format this year in favor of new challenges.

Questions spanning youth engagement, issues faced by Nepali women, ambitions and marriage, and Nepal's identity were asked and the finalists, with voices that echoed nothing but confidence, clarity and agency, answered the prompt questions.

A hush fell as the reigning titleholders took their farewell walk. Luna Luitel, Deepakshika Nepal, Urusha Bhandari and Sony Ghale, with their individual videos displayed on the stage's screen, reminisced what Miss Nepal meant to them, reflecting on their journeys, and the community and sisterhood they gained along the way.

Yet again, the show bounced back to the subtitle awards. ‘Yeti Airlines Women With Wings (Talent Show)’ was given to Bibhusha Basnet, ‘Creative D Studio Miss Photogenic’ to Yukta Paudel, and Deepmala Dhakal won ‘The Hidden Treasure Miss Beauty With a Purpose’.

Then, as the lighting built toward the stage as the grand crowning ceremony arrived. The night closed with the victory of these newly crowned titleholders in celebratory light as finalists, families, and guests spilled into an atmosphere of pure elation, bringing Miss Nepal's most reimagined season yet to a glittering close.

articles.title: Bhanubhakta beyond Ramayan: The other side of Nepal’s most revered poet
articles.summary:
This year’s Bhanu Jayanti came and went, as it does every year, without much controversy. The day saw celebratory poem-recitation competitions, extended morning assemblies in schools, and the general commemorations expected on the day.

Students, teachers and public figures alike spoke about Bhanubhakta’s translation of the Ramayan into Nepali and his general contributions to the language.

But 'Badhu Siksha’, Acharya’s prescriptive poem for the education of women, did not receive broad attention. In one stanza of the poem, Acharya instructs women to follow a life of devotion and service to their husbands, whom he says are no less than the gods. In another part, he warns that a woman who laughs risks becoming a beshya, a prostitute, and if not that, then risks at the least letting her house fall into disarray.

Ram Chandra Paudel, an associate professor of Nepali language and literature, who has been teaching for 25 years in Kathmandu University, shared that the poem was aimed at the wife and daughter-in-law of one of Bhanubhakta’s close friends, Tarapati. After witnessing the conflict-stricken state of Tarapati’s family affairs, he is said to have written the poem. Paudel also said that the poem is considered to be among Bhanubhakta’s minor works.

Bhushita Vasistha, a writer and researcher of Nepali and Sanskrit who recited Acharya’s ‘Badhu Sikshya’ with Nepalaya’s ‘Paleti’ in 2023, was the harshest in her criticism of the poem.

“I think the poem is degrading to women. The treatment of women in the poem is akin to that of livestock. Women are asked to contain their jealousy if their husband brings home another wife. There is no space for individuation and self-actualisation for women,” she said.

“Viewed from a modern feminist lens, there is definitely space to be critical of the poem. Nepal has always been a patriarchal society, one that is not critical of its men. Acharya does not comment on what his friend, Tarapati, himself could do better. If his house is in disarray, he must be part of the reason why, but he is not told what to do,” said Shiva Gopal Risal, an eminent professor of Nepali language and literature and author of 115 books. He was affiliated, for most of his career, with Padma Kanya Campus. Risal was among the first cohort of students to study Nepali at Tribhuvan University when it was established.

“Bhanu Bhakta’s poem is an example of the sort of education that women were given in his time. In particular, it is aimed at daughters-in-law. The prescriptions in the poem align with what many women's lives were like at the time. Even today, women might face similar expectations. Women at the time were, obviously, not going to school. They would get married off by their fathers into unfamiliar homes. At a time like that, when daughter-in-laws would have been beholden to their families, it was the only way to get by,” he added.

None of the experts were in favour of banning the work.

“People are not sheep. We need to have the courage to let people speak their mind. The sovereignty of the individual is the most important thing. We need to protect everybody’s freedom of speech,” Vasistha says.

“The poem is instructive. The mother-in-law is not the enemy of the daughter-in-law. She does not have to be cruel and suppressive, yet many mother-in-laws are. If the daughter-in-law does not protest, conflict is avoided. If she is of a nature where she won’t just take everything coming her way, there are problems. The poem is just as important today as it was when it was written. Ultimately, it teaches that women are not each other’s enemies, that they must learn to understand each other's problems,” Paudel said.

Experts also spoke of the value the poem carries.

“It is important because it is an archaeological history. It gives us rare insight into the society of the time. For example, the poem mentions Sati pratha; we learn then that Sati pratha was part of that society.” Additionally, Vasistha also praised the poem’s elegant use of meter.

“Like I said before, the poem is a living history in some ways. We are hearing the predominant opinion on these matters from a person of prominence and education in his time. Whatever one's views on the poem, it is important because it conveys some facts about society,” Risal said.

For example, in one part, the poem speaks of treating the members of the family to raisins, cashews and almonds. In another part, the poem speaks of how servants are to be dealt with. These lines tell readers that Tarapati would have been a rich man, that he had servants in his household and that people of his social class would have considered raisins, cashews and almonds to be special treats.

“The reason for this is the same as why Nepal’s bureaucracy has so many problems. People respect authority beyond reason. Acharya is a canonised figure in Nepal. People are not comfortable with criticising someone with the moniker of Adikavi”, Vasistha said.

Paudel shared that many of his students were unaware of who Bhanubhakta was, let alone be familiar with a minor work of his like ‘Badhu Sikshya’. Of readers who were familiar, he shared that readers were both respectful of his contributions and, in their place, critical of the poem for the same reasons that he was.

“With time, older ideas are challenged and fall out of fashion, the same thing is happening with ‘Badhu Sikshya', and it will continue to happen. This is not an extraordinary matter,” said Risal.

articles.title: A rom-com that learns to let go
articles.summary:
Eventually, Sharanya Rajgopal’s ‘Musafir Cafe’ settles into the cosiness of a novel found in a railway station bookstall. Those unintimidating 200-page paperbacks, which one buys for an overnight journey. Here, it happens in the seventh episode of this eight-episode series. Sudha (Vedika Pinto) is a pretty, impulsive, recklessly-ambitious girl from Bhopal – a version of a metropolitan idea of a small-town firebrand. The kind who discovered ‘Carpe Diem’ in her adolescence and never looked back. She has a job offer from Mumbai, which she reluctantly accepts.

Unfortunately, she’s in love with Chander (Vikrant Massey), who she met a few months ago, and is currently vacationing with, in Mussoorie. Chander, a US-returned engineer who harbours dreams of owning a cafe on a hill station, is the opposite of Sudha. He’s excited about Mussoorie, his boss has agreed to become his loan guarantor, and he might have also found a business partner.

Sudha hasn’t told Chander about her plans yet. And when she does – he quashes his plans, and talks about moving with her to Mumbai. This disappoints her. In a rather pragmatic moment in the show, Sudha shames Chander for flippantly giving up on his dreams, and choosing to follow her instead. Some of her respect diminishes for him. This scene is what the entire series is building towards – and it reveals a sincere relationship drama embedded within the glossy design of a staple Netflix rom-com.

Based on Divya Prakash Dubey’s novel of the same name, Rajgopal’s series doesn’t begin with the same assurance. There’s an inherent clash between the show’s earthy source material and the frothy, urban Netflix aesthetic (that makes Bhopal look like Andheri). The actors, Pinto as Sudha and Massey as Chander, look (and sound) very protagonist-y. They’re not ‘ordinary’ by any measure.

Chander has been asked to meet with Sudha at a cafe, as an arranged-marriage prospect. Sudha is transparently cruel as he tells him marriage is not on her radar, and that she does this to please her mother. Chander, a pragmatic nerd with low self-esteem, finds himself charmed by her lack of filter. An unsuccessful arranged marriage meet-up improvises into an unintentional first date.

Directed by Ruchir Arun, who spearheaded the walk-and-talk relationship dramas on India’s Youtube (like Little Things), even ‘Musafir Cafe’ has plenty of the genre’s ‘relatable’ affectations. Massey, usually an effortless actor, initially looks at sea with the narrative sparseness. There’s very little to Chander beyond his desire to get married, and his infatuation with Sudha. A quirk added for effect, where he’s particular about his coffee, never feels like an innate part of him. Pinto is unconvincing as a girl from Ratlam, especially with that body language that belongs in Soho House.

The humour, and the abrupt relationship expediency, feel contrived at first.

Things become more easy-going in the third and fourth episode

However, things become more easy-going in the third and fourth episode, when Chander’s mother (Anubha Fatehpuria), shows up unannounced. A scene featuring Sudha’s roommate, a staple scene in such shows, when the two girls giggle over Sudha’s brand-new partner, is cute.

Even though they’re hopelessly in love, they’re both aware it could be a fleeting thing. He wants to settle down in the hills, she wants to go to Mumbai and afford a life many only dream about. They’ve fundamentally opposite goals in life, something one will invariably have to ‘adjust’ for.

The more mature track unfolds in the present, (Chander & Sudha’s love story is shown to have taken place eight years before), where Chander has realised his dream of Musafir Cafe, in Mussoorie. It’s run by him and his partner, Preeti (Manisha Makhwana). It looks 3-D printed out of Instagram, given how there’s not a single smudge on the cafe’s table cloths.

The surprising detail here is that Preeti knows about Chander’s lack-of-closure with Sudha. She’s the generous lover, who rationalises her partner’s flaws on his behalf, and doesn’t allow any form of negativity. It’s an interesting relationship dynamic, where a woman patiently waits for her man to leave behind his past.

Preeti is so close to an ideal, and so plainly characterised, I’m tempted to call her an invention of the male gaze. Which is not to say, she’s not disarming. Makhwana plays the stoic Preeti using a light touch, who would rather silently suffer for her lover, than show signs of jealousy. When Sudha visits them in Mussoorie late in the show, she puts up a brave front as a host, and then weeps at home.

Like Preeti’s sadness here, the show fetishises some other things too. A writer character (Rajeev Siddhartha), who talks like he’s writing prose. Always dressed immaculately in dark overcoats, sipping tea/coffee as young girls (his fans) giggle around him, he doesn’t miss a beat flirting with Preeti (an aspiring writer, we’re told).

Also, the dream of owning a cafe in the hills feels like a very city-bred fantasy. There’s nothing to indicate that Chander and Preeti are struggling at all, as the cafe appears to be running itself. People come in, and speak in Instagram affirmations. ‘Musafir’ assumes an Imtiaz Ali metaphor for many, who look forward to the journey, rather than the destination. Most of them appear to be in search of themselves.

It could seem laughable from a distance, but I found myself smitten by the fantasy. It’s the kind of show where a business partner signs away his palatial chalet to Chander and Preeti before moving back to the US for good – which they can use for expansion.

After trudging along cliches of the will they/won’t they rom-com, ‘Musafir Cafe’ becomes the strongest version of itself in the final two episodes, when an older couple enters the picture. Played by Adil Hussain and Sadiya Siddiqui, they become the (high) benchmark for Chander.

As Sudha visits Chander one last time, before moving abroad for good, they have an awkward at first, but ultimately cathartic conversation, bringing closure to both of them. It’s a rare sight of exes being shown as both graceful and grateful around each other. If not for the relationship, they wouldn’t be the people they are today. Each failed relationship is also a coming-of-age tale. That’s a realisation few relationship dramas seem to have.

Arun and Rajgopal take a good call of ending things on a crescendo of ambiguity, rather than a neatly-tied climax with a slate of ‘The End’. It mimics the beats of a life that goes on long after the ‘story’ has concluded. I’d love for them to just leave it at that, instead of using the open end for a season two. Sometimes closure isn’t about certainty, it’s about knowing when to let go. Let’s hope Netflix does too.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.

articles.title: Nepali workers among injured in Qatar gas plant explosion, 13 killed
articles.summary:
Nepali workers were among those injured in an explosion and fire at a gas processing facility in Qatar, authorities said, as officials confirmed that 13 people were killed and 66 were injured in one of the country’s deadliest industrial accidents in recent years.

The blast occurred on Sunday night at the Barzan gas processing facility inside the Ras Laffan Industrial City complex, according to Qatar Energy officials. The injured include workers from Nepal, Qatar, India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Kenya, Ghana, Tanzania and Nigeria. Authorities said none of the injured is in a critical condition.

Energy minister and president and CEO of QatarEnergy, Saad bin Sherida al-Kaabi, said in Doha that the incident was a “technical accident” and not linked to sabotage or hostile activity. He said emergency teams and civil defence units brought the fire under control quickly.

Al-Kaabi said production at the Barzan facility had been halted for maintenance since December 2025 and was restarted only two days before the incident. He added that Qatar’s liquefied natural gas operations, export systems and port facilities were not affected.

The people killed were Indian and Pakistani nationals, he said.

Al-Kaabi said Qatar has sufficient gas reserves and alternative supply capacity, and the country’s export commitments will not be affected. He also expressed condolences to the families of the deceased and wished the injured a speedy recovery.

Authorities have launched an investigation into the cause of the explosion, Reuters reported.

Al-Kaabi said the incident is under review, while reiterating that there is no impact on wider energy infrastructure.

Qatar hosts one of the world’s largest liquefied natural gas export hubs at Ras Laffan.

articles.title: तराईका हिंसात्मक घटनामा सरकार र रास्वपाको भूमिकाप्रति शंकर पोखरेलको प्रश्न
articles.summary:
नेकपा (एमाले)का महासचिव शंकर पोखरेलले सुनसरी, सिराहा र धनुषालगायत तराईका विभिन्न स्थानमा धार्मिक तनावसँग जोडिएका हिंसात्मक घटनापछि भएको आन्दोलन तथा सरकार र राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा)बीच भएको वार्ताप्रति प्रश्न उठाएका छन्।

पोखरेलले रास्वपाले आफ्नै कार्यकर्तालाई आन्दोलनकारी बनाएर तिनैसँग वार्ता गरेर सम्झौता गरेको आरोप लगाउँदै प्रश्न उठाएका हुन्।

सोमबार सामाजिक सञ्जालमा लेख्दै उनले यस्तो आरोप लगाएका हुन्। उनले वार्तापछि हिंसाको दोष अरूमाथि थोपरेको भनाइ राखे।

'आफ्नै कार्यकर्तालाई आन्दोलनकारी बनाउने, तिनैसँग वार्ता गरेर सम्झौता गर्ने, अनि हिंसाको दोष चै अरूमाथि थोपर्ने यो जुक्ति गजबको छैन त?' उनले लेखेका छन्।

सुनसरीबाट सुरु भएको धार्मिक तनाव सिराहा, धनुषालगायत तराईका अन्य जिल्लामा फैलिँदा तीन जनाको मृत्यु भएको थियो भने कैयौँ घाइते भएका थिए। घटनापछि विभिन्न स्थानमा आन्दोलन, कर्फ्यु तथा वार्तामार्फत स्थिति सामान्य बनाउने प्रयास गरिएको थियो। सरकारले घटनाको छानबिन गरी दोषीमाथि कानुनबमोजिम कारबाही गर्ने प्रतिबद्धता जनाएको थियो भने विभिन्न राजनीतिक दल तथा सरोकारवालाले सामाजिक तथा धार्मिक सद्भाव कायम राख्न आह्वान गरेका थिए।

articles.title: सवारी साधनको ठक्करबाट वृद्धको मृत्यु
articles.summary:
झापाको कन्काई नगरपालिका–४ कोटीहोममा सवारी साधन ‘पिकअप’को ठक्करबाट एक वृद्धको मृत्यु भएको छ।

जिल्ला ट्राफिक कार्यालय झापाका अनुसार आज बिहान पूर्व–पश्चिम राजमार्गअन्तर्गत कोटीहोम क्षेत्रमा दमकबाट बिर्तामोडतर्फ आउँदै गरेको मे१च ५१०४ नम्बरको पिकअपले सडक पार गर्दै गरेका कन्काई–४ निवासी अन्दाजी ७० वर्षीय प्रल्हाद शिवाकोटीलाई ठक्कर दिएको हो।

दुर्घटनामा गम्भीर घाइते भएका शिवाकोटीलाई उपचारका लागि बिर्तामोडतर्फ ल्याउने क्रममा बाटोमा नै मृत्यु भएको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ। प्रहरीले दुर्घटनामा संलग्न पिकअप र त्यसका चालकलाई नियन्त्रणमा लिएको छ ।

articles.title: उपभोक्तालाई उपहारले लोभ्याएर करछली नियन्त्रणमा सरकार
articles.summary:
राजस्व संकलन वृद्धि र करछली नियन्त्रणका लागि अनेक उपाय अपनाउँदै आएको सरकारले अहिले उपभोक्तालाई उपहारले लोभ्याउने कार्यक्रम ल्याएको छ। सरकारले उपभोक्तालाई सामान खरिदको बिजक (बिल) मार्फत एक लाखदेखि १० लाख रुपैयाँसम्मको उपहार दिने व्यवस्था गरेर करछली नियन्त्रणमा नयाँ तरिका अपनाएको हो।

हाल बजारमा सामान किन्ने क्रममा उपभोक्ताले बिल माग्दा पनि व्यवसायीहरूले दिने गरेका छैनन्। केही व्यवसायीले त बिलको सट्टा भिजिटिङ कार्ड मात्र थमाउने गरेका छन्। सामान बिक्रीको बिल नै नदिई थोरै नाफा खाई मुलुकको कर प्रणाली र उपभोक्तालाई गुमराहमा राखेर व्यापार गर्दै आएका व्यवसायीलाई सरकारको यो उपायले केही असहज बनाउने देखिएको छ।

बजार अनुगमनका क्रममा व्यापारीबाट हुने यस्तो प्रवृत्तिको सुइँको पाएको आन्तरिक राजस्व विभागले करछली नियन्त्रण र वास्तविक कारोबार अभिलेखीकरण तथा उपभोक्तामा बिल लिने संस्कृतिको विकास गर्ने उद्देश्यले ‘करदाता प्रोत्साहन उपहार कार्यक्रम’ सञ्चालनमा ल्याएको हो।

बिल बुझाएकै आधारमा एक लाखदेखि १० लाख रुपैयाँसम्म पाउने यस आकर्षक उपहार योजनामा उपभोक्तालाई सहभागी गराएर बढीभन्दा बढी राजस्व उठाउने नयाँ उपाय अपनाएको विभागले देशभरका सम्पूर्ण सरोकारवालालाई अनिवार्य रूपमा बिल लिन आह्वान गरेको छ।

यस योजनालाई सफल बनाउन विभागले सार्वजनिक सूचना जारी गर्दै विभिन्न माध्यमबाट नगद कारोबार गरेका उपभोक्तालाई आफ्नो सक्कल बिल दर्ता गराउन आग्रह गरेको छ। विभागका उपमहानिर्देशक एवं सहसचिव जनकराज शर्माले यस्तो जानकारी गराएका हुन्।

विभागका अनुसार गत साउन १ देखि सय रुपैयाँभन्दा बढीको सामान वा सेवा नगदमा खरिद गरी सक्कल प्यान तथा मूल्य अभिवृद्धि कर (भ्याट) को बिल लिएका उपभोक्ता यस करदाता प्रोत्साहन कार्यक्रममा सहभागी हुन पाउने छन्। आफूले सामान खरिद गरेको बिल बुझाएकै आधारमा हरेक १५/१५ दिनमा एक लाख रुपैयाँ नगद पुरस्कार पाइने भएपछि धेरै उपभोक्ता यस कार्यक्रमतर्फ आकर्षित भएका छन्। यसबाट अहिलेको भन्दा बढी राजस्व संकलन हुने उपाय अपनाएर यस आकर्षक उपहार कार्यक्रममा उपभोक्तालाई सहभागी गराउन विभागले ‘प्राइज डट आइआरडी डट जिओभी डट एनपी’ नामक नयाँ वेबसाइट नै सञ्चालनमा ल्याएको छ।

शनिबारबाट सञ्चालनमा आएको उक्त वेबसाइटबारे जानकारी गराउँदै विभागका उपमहानिर्देशक शर्माले भने, ‘नगद भुक्तानी गरी स्वप्रयोजनका लागि मुलुकभित्र एकपटकमा सय रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी मूल्यको वस्तु तथा सेवा खरिद गर्ने बिल लिएका योग्य उपभोक्ताले यस वेबसाइटमा गएर आफ्नो बिल अपलोड गर्न सक्ने छन्।’

यसैगरी क्युआरमार्फत गरिने कारोबारमा भने स्वतः कर प्रणालीमार्फत नै यस आकर्षक उपहार कार्यक्रमको प्रणालीमा समावेश गरिसकिएको जनाइएको छ। क्युआरमार्फत भुक्तानी गरेका उपभोक्ताले बिल प्रविष्टि (इन्ट्री) गर्नुपर्ने आवश्यकता विभागले स्पष्ट पारेको छ।

त्यस्तै बैंक तथा वालेटको क्युआरमार्फत सय रुपैयाँभन्दा बढीको वस्तु तथा सेवा खरिद गरेका उपभोक्ताले पनि अहिले बिल दर्ता गराउनुनपर्ने व्यवस्था मिलाइएको विभागले जनाएको छ। क्युआरबाट पैसा तिरेको कारोबार डाउनलोड गरेर राख्ने र सोही ट्रान्जेक्सन नम्बर’ नै उपहारका लागि विभागको प्रणालीमा प्रविष्ट भइसकेकाले सो नम्बर नै उपहारका लागि योग्य हुने विभागले स्पष्ट पारेको छ। तर उपहार घोषणापछि सक्कल बिल अनिवार्य हुने भएकाले त्यसलाई सुरक्षित राख्न विभागले उपभोक्तालाई ध्यानाकर्षण गराएको छ।

लोभलाग्दो यस कार्यक्रमलाई पूर्ण रूपमा कार्यान्वयनमा ल्याउन विभागले आफूले गरेको खरिदको सक्कल भ्याट तथा प्यान बिल व्यापारीसँग माग्न र बिल नपाएको खण्डमा विभागमा जानकारी गराउनसमेत आम उपभोक्तालाई आग्रह गरेको छ। त्यसका लागि विभागले साउन १ देखि लागु गरेको करदाता प्रोत्साहन कार्यक्रमको पहिलो १५ दिनको नतिजा यही साता सार्वजनिक गर्ने तयारी गरेको बताएको छ। यसै साता पहिलो १५ दिनको (हरेक दिनको एक लाख रुपैयाँका दरले १५ जना विजेता र १५ दिनको बम्पर १० लाखको विजेता एक जना) छनोटको नतिजा घोषणा हुने विभागले जनाएको छ।

यसअघि सरकारले चालु आर्थिक वर्ष २०८३/८४ को बजेटमार्फत हरेक करदातालाई कर प्रणालीमा ल्याउन र बिल लिने संस्कृतिको विकास गर्न ‘करदाता प्रोत्साहन उपहार कार्यक्रम’ सञ्चालन गर्ने घोषणा गरेको थियो। बजेट सार्वजनिक गर्ने क्रममा अर्थमन्त्री डा. स्वर्णिम वाग्लेले गरेको सोही घोषणाअनुसार मन्त्रालयले गत असार अन्तिम साता ‘उपहार सञ्चालन कार्यविधि २०८३’ स्वीकृत गरेको थियो। सोही कार्यविधिअनुसार हरेक दिन एक उपभोक्तालाई करकट्टी गरेर एक लाख रुपैयाँ नगद र हरेक १५–१५ दिनमा (महिनाको दुई जनालाई) बम्पर उपहारस्वरूप १० लाख रुपैयाँ नगद प्रदान गरिने विभागले जनाएको छ। यसअघि गत बिहीबार नेपाल राष्ट्र बैंकले करदाता प्रोत्साहन उपहार कार्यक्रमलाई सहजीकरण गर्न भुक्तानी सेवा प्रदायकहरूलाई निर्देशन दिएको थियो। राष्ट्र बैंकले सरकारले सञ्चालन गर्न लागेको ‘करदाता प्रोत्साहन उपहार कार्यक्रम’लाई व्यवस्थित र प्रभावकारी बनाउन भुक्तानी सेवा प्रदायक संस्थाहरूलाई निर्देशन दिएको छ।

राष्ट्र बैंक, भुक्तानी प्रणाली विभागले भुक्तानीसम्बन्धी कार्य गर्न अनुमति प्राप्त सबै संस्थालाई पत्राचार गर्दै आन्तरिक राजस्व विभाग सञ्चालन गर्ने कार्यक्रमका लागि विद्युतीय प्रणालीमा अन्तर–आबद्धता कायम गर्न र कार्यक्रमकाबारे ग्राहकलाई समयमै सूचित गर्न भनेको छ। यसका लागि सबै भुक्तानी सेवा प्रदायकले आफ्नो मोबाइल एपमा उपहार कार्यक्रमसँग सम्बन्धित बारम्बार सोधिने प्रश्नहरूको एउटा छुट्टै खण्ड समावेश गर्नुपर्ने छ।

आगामी बिहीबार उपहार वितरण सुरु हुने यस कार्यक्रमबारे पूर्वजानकारी दिन आफ्ना सबै ग्राहकलाई मोबाइल एपमार्फत नोटिफिकेसन पठाउनुपर्ने राष्ट्र बैंकको निर्देशनमा उल्लेख छ। यस कार्यक्रममा सहभागी हुन ग्राहकले आफ्नो मोबाइल एप अपडेट गर्नुपर्ने भए त्यसको जानकारीसमेत नोटिफिकेसनमार्फत नै दिनुपर्ने नियम बनाइएको राष्ट्र बैंकले जनाएको छ।

राष्ट्र बैंकको सो निर्देशन र आन्तरिक राजस्व विभागको यस्तो नयाँ उपायबाट अब सामान वा सेवा खरिद गरी बिल लिँदा उपहार पाउने लोभमा कति उपभोक्ता सहभागी हुने छन् भनेर कार्यक्रम सञ्चालनको क्रममा बिस्तारै देखिँदै जाने छ। बजारमा सामान किन्दा उपभोक्ताले बिल माग्दा नदिएर उल्टै भिजिटिङ कार्ड थमाएर व्यापार गर्दै आएका अधिकांश व्यवसायीलाई भने बिल जारी गर्नुपर्ने यो सरकारी नियमले केही अप्ठ्यारो बनाउने छ।

हाल बजारमा देखिएका करछली तथा वास्तविक बिल नै जारी नगरी राजस्व छल्दै आएका हजारौं व्यवसायीबाट करोडौं रुपैयाँ कर उठाउने उद्देश्यले सरकारले यो ‘करदाता प्रोत्साहन उपहार कार्यक्रम’ सञ्चालनमा ल्याएको विभागले जनाएको छ।

अहिलेको भन्दा धेरै कर उठाउने लक्ष्य लिएर कार्यान्वयनमा ल्याइएको यस्तो उपभोक्ता लोभ्याउने उपहार जित्ने कार्यक्रम सञ्चालनका क्रममा उपभोक्ता स्वयंले व्यापारीसँग सहजै अनिवार्य बिल माग्ने वातावरण बन्ने विभागको दाबी छ। सय रुपैयाँभन्दा बढीको सामान वा सेवा खरिद गर्दा बिल लिएर लक्की ड्रमार्फत उपहार पाउने सरकारी योजना सुरु भएपछि सरकारले विगतका वर्षहरूमा भन्दा धेरै राजस्व उठाउने लक्ष्य लिएको हो। सोही लक्ष्य प्राप्तिका लागि सरकारले ‘करदाता प्रोत्साहन उपहार कार्यक्रम–२०८३’ कार्यान्वयनमा ल्याउँदै दैनिक एक लाख रुपैयाँ र हरेक १५ दिनमा १० लाख रुपैयाँ नगद पुरस्कार जित्ने मौका दिएको छ।

आन्तरिक राजस्व विभागले नगद भुक्तानी गरी आफ्नै प्रयोजनका लागि नेपालभित्र एक पटकमा सय रुपैयाँभन्दा बढी मूल्यका वस्तु वा सेवा खरिद गरी कर बिजक लिएका अन्तिम उपभोक्ताले विभागको वेबसाइटमा खरिद विवरण प्रविष्ट गरी यस कार्यक्रममा सहभागी हुन सक्ने बताएको छ।

यस कार्यक्रमका लागि छुट्टै ‘अनलाइन पोर्टल’ नै सञ्चालनमा ल्याएर यस्तो मौका दिएको विभागले जनाएको छ।

विभागका अनुसार यस कार्यक्रममा सहभागी उपभोक्ताले वस्तु वा सेवा खरिद गर्दा प्राप्त कर बिजक दर्ता गरी पुरस्कार कुपन प्राप्त गर्न सक्ने छन्। आफूले सामान खरिद गरेको बिल वेबसाइटमा विवरण प्रविष्ट गरेपछि ‘उपहार कुपन’ स्वतः उत्पन्न हुने छ। सोही कुपनमा रहेको नम्बर लक्की ड्रमा समावेश हुने छ। विजेता घोषणापछि सम्बन्धित बिलको फोटो र आवश्यक विवरण पेस गरेर पुरस्कार दाबी गर्न सकिने विभागले बताएको छ। जसका लागि नगद र विद्युतीय भुक्तानीका लागि फरक व्यवस्था गरिएको विभागले जनाएको छ।

नगदमा भुक्तानी गरी खरिद गर्ने उपभोक्ताले बिल नम्बर, बिक्रेताको प्यान नम्बर, बिल जारी भएको मिति, तिरेको कुल रकम तथा आफ्नो नाम, मोबाइल नम्बर र ठेगाना प्रविष्ट गरी बिल दर्ता गर्नुपर्ने छ।

यसैगरी क्युआर कोड वा भिसाकार्डमार्फत गरिएको विद्युतीय भुक्तानी स्वतः प्रणालीमा समावेश हुने भएकाले छुट्टै विवरण भर्नुपर्ने छैन। यस कार्यक्रम पूर्ण रूपमा कार्यान्वयनमा ल्याउन राष्ट्र बैंकले ई–सेवा, खल्तीलगायत विभिन्न अनुमतिप्राप्त डिजिटल भुक्तानी सेवा प्रदायकलाई आवश्यक प्राविधिक सहजीकरण गर्नसमेत निर्देशन दिइसकेको छ।

यस कार्यक्रममा सहभागी हुनेले जाली, सच्याइएको, दोहोरिएको, झुटा वा अनधिकृत बिल पेस गरे प्रविष्टि अस्वीकृत हुने, पुरस्कार कुपन रद्द गरिने, वितरण भइसकेको पुरस्कारसमेत फिर्ता असुल गरिने र प्रचलित कानुनबमोजिम कारबाही हुन सक्ने चेतावनी दिइएको छ । डिजिटल भुक्तानीबाट प्राप्त हुने पुरस्कार कुपन कोड सम्बन्धित बैंक वा डिजिटल वालेट एपको कारोबार विवरण, सूचना, कुपन वा रिवार्ड सेक्सनमा हेर्न सकिने विभागले जनाएको छ।

articles.title: धार्मिक तथा सामाजिक सद्भाव कायम गर्न राष्ट्रिय संवादको माग
articles.summary:
विश्व शान्ति तथा अध्यात्म विज्ञान समाज नेपालले नेपालमा धार्मिक, सांस्कृतिक तथा सामाजिक सद्भाव, राष्ट्रिय एकता, सहिष्णुता र शान्तिको वातावरण थप सुदृढ बनाउन सबै नेपालीसँग अपिल गरेको छ।

जारी प्रेस विज्ञप्तिमा समाजले नेपाल भगवान् बुद्धको जन्मभूमि, भगवान् शिवको तपोभूमि तथा बहुधार्मिक सहअस्तित्वको अनुपम भूमि भएकाले विश्वलाई शान्ति, करुणा र मानवताको सन्देश दिँदै आएको उल्लेख गरेको छ। यस गौरवपूर्ण पहिचानको संरक्षण गर्नु सबै नेपालीको साझा दायित्व भएको समाजको भनाइ छ।

पछिल्लो समय धर्म वा आस्थाका नाममा बढ्दै गएको असहिष्णुता र सामाजिक तनावप्रति गम्भीर चिन्ता व्यक्त गर्दै धर्मको मूल उद्देश्य विभाजन नभई प्रेम, करुणा, सत्य, क्षमा र शान्तिको प्रवर्द्धन गर्नु रहेको विज्ञप्तिमा उल्लेख गरिएको छ।

समाजले नेपाल सरकारसँग सबै धर्मका धार्मिक अगुवा, विद्वान्, नागरिक समाज तथा सरोकारवालाको सहभागितामा राष्ट्रिय संवाद तत्काल सुरु गर्न आग्रह गरेको छ। यस्तै, सनातन, बौद्ध, किराँत, इस्लाम, क्रिश्चियन, सिख, जैनलगायत सबै धर्म र आस्थाका अनुयायीलाई एकअर्काको विश्वासको सम्मान गर्दै सामाजिक सद्भाव, सहअस्तित्व र राष्ट्रिय एकतालाई थप मजबुत बनाउन आह्वान गरिएको छ।

आवश्यकता परे निष्पक्ष, समावेशी र शान्तिपूर्ण संवादको सहजीकरण तथा समन्वयमा विश्व शान्ति तथा अध्यात्म विज्ञान समाज नेपाल पूर्ण रूपमा सहयोग गर्न तयार रहेको पनि विज्ञप्तिमा उल्लेख छ।

समाजले सम्पूर्ण नेपालीलाई घृणा र विभाजनभन्दा माथि उठेर प्रेम, सहिष्णुता र मानवताका साझा मूल्यलाई आत्मसात् गर्दै समृद्ध, शान्तिपूर्ण र सभ्य नेपाल निर्माणमा हातेमालो गर्न आग्रह गरेको छ। साथै, 'हामी पहिले नेपाली हौं' भन्ने भावनालाई आत्मसात् गर्दै नेपाललाई शान्ति र अध्यात्मको केन्द्रका रूपमा पुनः स्थापित गर्न सबै पक्षलाई एकजुट हुन आह्वान गरिएको छ।

articles.title: तराईका हिंसात्मक घटनामा सरकार र रास्वपाको भूमिकाप्रति शंकर पोखरेलको प्रश्न
articles.summary:
नेकपा (एमाले)का महासचिव शंकर पोखरेलले सुनसरी, सिराहा र धनुषालगायत तराईका विभिन्न स्थानमा धार्मिक तनावसँग जोडिएका हिंसात्मक घटनापछि भएको आन्दोलन तथा सरकार र राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा)बीच भएको वार्ताप्रति प्रश्न उठाएका छन्।

पोखरेलले रास्वपाले आफ्नै कार्यकर्तालाई आन्दोलनकारी बनाएर तिनैसँग वार्ता गरेर सम्झौता गरेको आरोप लगाउँदै प्रश्न उठाएका हुन्।

सोमबार सामाजिक सञ्जालमा लेख्दै उनले यस्तो आरोप लगाएका हुन्। उनले वार्तापछि हिंसाको दोष अरूमाथि थोपरेको भनाइ राखे।

'आफ्नै कार्यकर्तालाई आन्दोलनकारी बनाउने, तिनैसँग वार्ता गरेर सम्झौता गर्ने, अनि हिंसाको दोष चै अरूमाथि थोपर्ने यो जुक्ति गजबको छैन त?' उनले लेखेका छन्।

सुनसरीबाट सुरु भएको धार्मिक तनाव सिराहा, धनुषालगायत तराईका अन्य जिल्लामा फैलिँदा तीन जनाको मृत्यु भएको थियो भने कैयौँ घाइते भएका थिए। घटनापछि विभिन्न स्थानमा आन्दोलन, कर्फ्यु तथा वार्तामार्फत स्थिति सामान्य बनाउने प्रयास गरिएको थियो। सरकारले घटनाको छानबिन गरी दोषीमाथि कानुनबमोजिम कारबाही गर्ने प्रतिबद्धता जनाएको थियो भने विभिन्न राजनीतिक दल तथा सरोकारवालाले सामाजिक तथा धार्मिक सद्भाव कायम राख्न आह्वान गरेका थिए।

articles.title: अफवाह होइन सद्भावमा अग्रसरता, सामाजिक–राजनीतिक अगुवा सार्वजनिक आह्वानमा सक्रिय
articles.summary:
सुनसरी । सुनसरीमा दुई समुदायबीच भएको झडपपछि विभिन्न जिल्लामा फैलिएको तनावका बीच कोशी–मधेशका विभिन्न सहरमा सामाजिक सद्भाव र धार्मिक सहिष्णुताको सन्देश दिँदै बृहत् सद्भाव ¥याली आयोजना गरिदैछ । देशका विभिन्न स्थानमा निकालिएका यस्ता ¥यालीले सामाजिक सद्भाव कायम हुने ठानिएको छ ।

सुनसरीमा भएको घटनापछि मधेशका विभिन्न जिल्लामा देखिएको तनावका बीच सामाजिक सद्भाव कायम गर्ने उद्देश्यले बृहत् सद्भाव ¥याली निकालिएको छ । जिल्ला प्रशासन कार्यालय धनुषाको अगुवाइमा आयोजित ¥याली जनकपुरधामस्थित रेल्वे स्टेशनबाट शुरु भइ नगरका विभिन्न मुख्य सडक हुँदै सम्पन्न भएको थियो ।

¥यालीमा राजनीतिक दलका प्रतिनिधि, सुरक्षा निकाय, स्थानीय तहका जनप्रतिनिधि, धार्मिक अगुवा, नागरिक समाज तथा उद्योगी–व्यवसायीहरूको उल्लेख्य सहभागिता रहेको थियो ।

धनुषाका प्रमुख जिल्ला अधिकारी प्रेमप्रसाद लुइँटेलले मिथिला सभ्यता र संस्कृतिले सधैँ शान्ति, सहिष्णुता र सद्भावको सन्देश दिएको उल्लेख गर्दै सामाजिक एकता जोगाउन सबैलाई जिम्मेवार र संयमित बन्न आग्रह गरे ।

नेपाली कम्युनिष्ट पार्टीका केन्द्रीय सदस्य दीपक यादवले सामाजिक सद्भाव कायम राख्न सबै समुदाय एकजुट हुनुपर्ने बताउँदै सुनसरी र सिरहाका घटनाको निष्पक्ष छानबिन गरी दोषीमाथि कारबाही गर्न माग गरे ।

जनकपुरधाम उपमहानगरपालिकाका पूर्वउपमेयर असगर अलीले घटनाबाट प्रभावितलाई न्याय दिलाउनुका साथै समाजमा विश्वास र सद्भाव कायम गर्न समुदायबीच निरन्तर संवाद आवश्यक रहेको बताए ।

यता, मोरङको लेटाङ नगरपालिकाका नगर प्रमुख भुपेन्द्र कुमार लावतीले २०६५ साल देखि नै लेटाङमा अन्तरधार्मिक शान्ति संजाल गठन गरेर सबै धर्म र जातजाति बीच सामाजिक सद्भाव कायम गर्राईरहेको जानकारी दिए ।

सामाजिक सञ्जालमा देखिने विभिन्न अफवाहलाई रोक्दै सद्भाव कायम गर्नुपर्ने गरि सार्वजनिक अपिल गर्न थालिएको छ। केहिदिनदेखि अशान्त बनेको तराई मधेसमा विस्तारै शान्ति स्थापनाका निम्ति नागरिक नै जागरुक बन्न थालेका छन्। यद्यपी वीरगञ्ज र सिरहाको गोलबजारलगायतका केही क्षेत्रमा भने निषेधाज्ञा अझै कायम रहेको प्रशासनले जनाएको छ ।

articles.title: शैलेन्द्र अधिकारीको तेस्रो उपन्यास ‘तेजस्’ सार्वजनिक
articles.summary:
काठमाडौँ । लेखक तथा अध्यापक शैलेन्द्र अधिकारीको तेस्रो उपन्यास ‘तेजस्’ सार्वजनिक भएको छ। शनिबार एक कार्यक्रमबीच बुद्धविहार काठमाडौँका भिक्षु कोण्डन्य, आख्यानकार एवं अनलाइनखबरका प्रधान सम्पादक बसन्त बस्नेत, संस्कृतिकर्मी नानी हेरा शाक्य, राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा)का नेता मिलन पाण्डे र कवि रुपक अलंकारलले पुस्तकको संयुक्त विमोचन गरेका हुन्।

कार्यक्रममा भिक्षु कोण्डन्यले ‘तेजस्’मा राणाकालमा बौद्ध समुदायमाथि भएको दमन र भिक्षुहरूलाई देशनिकाला गरिएको प्रसंग तथा पञ्चायतकालमा उनीहरू स्वदेश फर्किएको इतिहासलाई समेटिएको बताए।

उपन्यासले भाषा, संस्कार र संस्कृतिको संरक्षणको सशक्त सन्देश दिएको उनको भनाइ थियो। विपश्यना र बौद्ध दर्शनका पक्षहरू पनि कथामा प्रभावकारी रूपमा समेटिएको भन्दै उनले उपन्यास सशक्त र पठनीय भएको बताए ।

आख्यानकार एवं अनलाइनखबरका प्रधान सम्पादक बस्नेतले ‘तेजस्’ काठमाडौँको भूगोल र इतिहास बुझ्न अत्यन्त उपयोगी कृति भएको बताए।

सेतो ख्याकको दृष्टिकोणबाट कथा भनिएकाले उपन्यास रहस्यमय बनेको उल्लेख गर्दै उनले बौद्ध धर्ममाथि राज्यले विभिन्न कालखण्डमा गरेको उपेक्षा र दमनलाई पुस्तकले गहिराइका साथ उजागर गरेको उनको भनाइ थियो। ‘कान्तिपुर (काठमाडौँ) को भूगोल र इतिहासको यो एउटा टुर गाइड पुस्तक बनेको छ,’ उनले भने, ‘किताब स्वादको बनेको छ। संगठन नबनाइ एक्लै एक्लै काम गर्दा बिद्धस्टहरूलाई राज्यले कति सतायो भन्ने दस्तावेज हो यो किताब।

रास्वपा नेता पाण्डेले असन, वसन्तपुर, नेवार समुदाय र ख्याकसँग सम्बन्धित धेरै कम सुनिएका कथा पुस्तकमा समेटिएको उल्लेख गर्दै उपन्यासले काठमाडौँका सम्पदालाई हेर्ने आफ्नो दृष्टिकोण नै परिवर्तन गरेको बताए।

संस्कृतिविद् नानीहेरा शाक्यले उपन्यासले नेपाल मण्डलकालीन कान्तिपुर, वसन्तपुर, कुमारीघर र चित्लाङसम्मको परिवेशलाई जीवन्त रूपमा उतारेको बताइन्। नेवार समुदाय कसरी क्रमशः सीमान्तकृत भयो भन्ने विषयलाई संवेदनशील ढंगले प्रस्तुत गरिएको भन्दै उनले नेपाल भाषाका केही शब्दमा सामान्य त्रुटि रहेको पनि औंल्याइन्।

कवि रूपक अलंकारले अध्ययनशील लेखकका रूपमा अधिकारीको प्रशंसा गर्दै ‘तेजस्’ कुनै एक पात्रको कथा मात्र नभई समयसँगै बदलिएको काठमाडौँ, नेवारी संस्कृति र बौद्ध धर्मको रूपान्तरणको कथा भएको बताए। शाहकाल र त्यसपछिका राजनीतिक परिवर्तनले काठमाडौँ र बौद्ध परम्परामा पारेको प्रभावलाई उपन्यासले प्रभावशाली रूपमा चित्रण गरेको उनको भनाइ थियो।

लेखक शैलेन्द्र अधिकारीले उपन्यास लेख्ने क्रममा नेपालबाट बौद्ध भिक्षुहरू देशनिकाला गरिएको इतिहासले आफूलाई गहिरो रूपमा छोएको बताए। नेवारी समुदायको जीवन र संस्कृतिलाई नजिकबाट बुझ्न आफूले लामो समय अध्ययन र सहकार्य गरेको उल्लेख गर्दै उनले इतिहास, मिथक र सामाजिक यथार्थलाई जोडेर ‘तेजस्’ तयार भएको उनको भनाइ थियो।

शिखा बुक्सले प्रकाशन गरेको पुस्तकको मूल्य ७२५ रुपैयाँ तोकिएको छ।

articles.title: Tensions flare in Susta after Indian personnel dismantle flood barrier
articles.summary:
Tensions resurfaced along the disputed Nepal-India border in Nawalparasi West on Sunday after Indian security personnel crossed into Nepali territory and dismantled a makeshift embankment that residents had built to protect their village from flooding, prompting a confrontation with locals.

The incident comes just two months after Indian border personnel halted the construction of a permanent flood-control embankment being built by the government in the same area.

Videos circulating on social media show heated exchanges between residents of Susta in Nawalparasi West district and men identified by locals as Indian security personnel.

According to residents, a group of Indian personnel in plain clothes entered Nepali territory carrying spades and began digging up an earthen embankment that villagers had recently built to reduce the risk of floodwaters from the Narayani river inundating the settlement.

Residents rushed to stop them, triggering a standoff before Nepal’s Armed Police Force intervened to prevent the situation from escalating.

“We came together to stop Indian security personnel as soon as we saw them entering our land,” said resident Sarar Sah. “We protested as they arrived with spades and began destroying the embankment.”

He said the Armed Police Force later calmed the situation.

Residents say they could not remain silent while foreign security personnel entered Nepali territory and damaged structures built to protect their homes. A video filmed by Sah has since gone viral online.

Rabindra Jaiswal, spokesperson for the Susta Protection Campaign, said villagers had constructed the temporary earthen embankment only after Indian authorities blocked Nepal from building a permanent flood-control structure along the Narayani river.

“When the permanent embankment was stopped, residents piled up earth as a temporary measure to reduce flood risks,” he said. “Indian security personnel in plain clothes then crossed over and began digging it up.”

Chief District Officer Dipak Raj Nepal confirmed that a dispute had broken out between residents and Indian security personnel over the embankment. He said officials from both sides are expected to hold discussions on Monday in an effort to resolve the issue.

Long-running border dispute

The latest confrontation highlights the unresolved territorial dispute surrounding Susta, one of the most sensitive stretches of the Nepal-India border.

While 16 border pillars mark most of the Nepal-India boundary in Nawalparasi West, none exist along the roughly 24-kilometre Susta stretch.

Instead, the two countries rely on natural features such as rivers and trees to indicate the boundary, leading to recurring disputes over land ownership and cultivation. A silk cotton tree currently serves as the de facto boundary marker in part of the disputed area.

Residents say the Narayani river’s changing course over decades has further complicated the border.

Sunday’s incident follows a similar dispute on May 31, when India’s Border Security Force (SSB) entered ward 5 of Susta Rural Municipality and objected to the construction of a permanent embankment being built by Nepal’s Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation.

The Rs140 million project aims to protect settlements from erosion and flooding.

Residents said about a dozen Indian security personnel arrived at the construction site and warned workers not to continue.

According to Chief District Officer Nepal, the dispute centred on a new 132-metre section of embankment planned about 50 metres east of an existing structure, still within Nepali territory.

Hari Pant, the engineer overseeing the project, said Indian security personnel, who arrived in uniform, instructed workers to stop construction before leaving.

Jaiswal said Indian authorities had objected specifically to the 132-metre extension, despite the broader project covering about one kilometre along the river.

The embankment project was launched after former Energy Minister Kulman Ghising visited Susta eight months ago and directed authorities to prioritise flood protection for the vulnerable settlement.

Susta is surrounded by the Narayani river to the north and west and India’s Bihar state to the south and east.

India maintains three SSB outposts near the area, while Nepal has a Border Security Post staffed by the Armed Police Force under the command of an inspector.

Residents say Indian authorities have repeatedly challenged Nepal’s activities in the area, citing the absence of clearly demarcated border pillars.

Historical roots

Susta has been at the centre of Nepal-India border tensions for decades.

In 1965, then-King Mahendra settled around 400 families, including retired soldiers, in the area to strengthen Nepal’s presence along the frontier.

Residents say Indian authorities opposed the settlement from the beginning.

In 1970, an Indian group reportedly chased away a Nepali government team that had travelled to distribute land ownership certificates. Nepal later deployed police to complete land surveys and issue titles to roughly 400 families by 1974.

However, after the Narayani river changed course in 1977, much of the settlement turned into riverbed, forcing many residents to relocate. Locals say India has since taken advantage of the shifting river and the absence of permanent border markers to expand its presence.

Adam Kha, acting chairman of the Susta Protection Campaign, said residents have little confidence in district-level meetings between Nepali and Indian officials.

“Can a meeting between district administrators resolve an international boundary dispute?” he said. “People who know Susta best are rarely included in these discussions. The issue requires a high-level bilateral mechanism backed by historical records and proper boundary surveys.”

Security concerns intensify

Repeated confrontations over the embankment have prompted Nepal to strengthen its security presence in Susta.

Over the past two months, senior officials from the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force and Nepal Police have visited the area to assess the situation.

The home ministry has also instructed district authorities to address long-standing concerns raised by residents, including difficulties in obtaining citizenship certificates.

One visit by senior Nepali Army officers in plain clothes drew particular attention from the Indian side.

According to a senior Nepali security official, Indian security personnel questioned the purpose of the team’s presence after noticing unfamiliar faces in the border village.

“They were naturally curious when they saw new people in such a sensitive area,” the official said.

The inspection team, led by senior Nepali Army officer Yam Bahadur Adhikari, visited Susta on July 6 to assess conditions on the ground.

Brigadier General Rajaram Basnet, spokesperson for the Nepali Army, said thesaid the visit was part of nationwide assessments of monsoon-related disaster risks and had no other objective.

“It was purely to assess monsoon and disaster risks,” Basnet said.

Armed Police Force Additional Inspector General Anjani Pokharel and Lumbini Province Police Chief Deputy Inspector General Bhupendra Bahadur Khatri have also inspected the area separately.

Nepal has increased the number of Armed Police personnel stationed in Susta from 25 to 40 in response to growing tensions.

Residents seek stronger protection

Residents have stepped up pressure on the government to improve security and address long-standing administrative problems.

Two weeks ago, 52 residents led by Susta campaigner Munna Kha travelled to Kathmandu and staged a protest at Maitighar Mandala, demanding stronger state protection.

During a meeting with Home Minister Sudan Gurung, they urged the government to establish a Nepali Army security post in Susta, alleging years of harassment by Indian security personnel.

Following the meeting, the home ministry instructed the district administration to reinforce security in sensitive areas of Susta and to begin processing citizenship applications for eligible residents who lack citizenship documents.

Local authorities say work has already begun to compile the necessary records for issuing citizenship certificates to eligible residents.

articles.title: Surging food prices pile pressure on consumers as festivals approach
articles.summary:
Households across Nepal are struggling with a sharp rise in the cost of daily essentials, as the prices of rice, edible oil, pulses, vegetables and eggs continue to climb, stretching family budgets just months before the Dashain and Tihar festivals.

While traders attribute the increases to higher import costs, seasonal supply shortages and rising transport expenses, consumer rights advocates say weak market oversight has allowed unjustified price hikes to go unchecked. They argue that inadequate monitoring has created room for profiteering at a time when demand for essential goods traditionally begins to rise.

The increase in food prices comes as consumers are also grappling with an artificial shortage of cooking gas in several parts of the country, adding to concerns over the rising cost of living.

Rice, the country's staple food, has seen some of the steepest increases, with retail prices rising by as much as Rs400 per bag over the past three months.

Vibhor Agrawal, executive director of Radhakrishna Rice Mills and a member of the Nepal Rice, Oil and Pulses Producers Association, said the increase was primarily driven by rising procurement costs in India. Nepal purchases large quantities of paddy from the southern neighbour.

“The price of paddy in India has increased by 800 to 900 Indian rupees per quintal,” Agrawal said. “Once transport costs, milling expenses and customs duties are added, the increase is reflected in retail prices.”

According to Agrawal, a bag of Jira Masino rice that sold for around Rs2,100 three months ago now costs about Rs2,500.
